analysis: What changed versus the 5:00 AM brief: the split widened, not narrowed. Dow futures held +0.7% and the S&P stayed faintly positive, but Nasdaq-100 futures slipped to -0.8% as the chip selloff deepened — Qualcomm fell further to -12.1% premarket and at least eight brokerages cut price targets, while AMD, Arm, Marvell and Micron all fell 3% or more. Nvidia actually steadied a touch (-1.4% vs -1.8% at 5 AM), so the damage is concentrated in the memory/handset and AI-infrastructure names rather than the whole complex. The fresh macro item is the jobless-claims print: 189K, a 57-year low versus 196K expected, which keeps the resilient-labor story intact into Friday's payrolls and gives the Fed no new reason to hurry. A new angle on the data-center trade also landed: Reuters reports the Democratic sweep is raising concerns about hurdles to rapid data-center expansion, with IREN, Hut 8 and Applied Digital down 1.1-2.7% — a political overhang on the buildout, distinct from the memory-cost margin story. The counterweight is AppLovin: a genuine earnings blowout (+55% revenue, raised Q4 guide, $3.2B buyback) that sent the stock +24% premarket, while Dutch Bros showed the other side of earnings season — a beat punished (-14.5%) on a cut outlook. Signal vs noise: the Dow/S&P-vs-Nasdaq split, the Qualcomm-led chip margin squeeze, the claims beat and the data-center political overhang are signal; single-name earnings reactions (AppLovin, Dutch Bros, Cava) are noise for the index tape. No qualifying Hacker News or Reddit threads surfaced — HN results were stale and the Reddit search returned nothing — so community_signals is empty rather than padded.
disclaimer: Not financial advice — for informational purposes only.

headlines.headline: Futures are still split 30 minutes before the open: Dow futures up about 0.7%, S&P 500 futures up 0.1% and Nasdaq-100 futures down about 0.8%, after Wednesday's rally (Dow +3.03% to 53,356.12, S&P +1.58% to 7,688.62, Nasdaq +1.44% to 25,736.51).
headlines.why_it_matters: The rotation is holding into the open — the Dow is still improving while the Nasdaq slides, so breadth is carrying the tape while tech drags.

headlines.headline: Initial jobless claims fell 6,000 to 189,000 for the week ended October 31, below the 196,000 economists expected and matching the mid-July level — the lowest reading since 1969, a 57-year low. Claims have stayed mostly below 200,000 since mid-September. Continuing claims rose 23,000 to 1.718 million; Challenger reported 43,994 announced job cuts in October, up 2% from September.
headlines.why_it_matters: A resilient-labor print removes a recession worry heading into the open and into Friday's payrolls — it gives the market no new reason to price a faster Fed easing path.

headlines.headline: Qualcomm deepened its slide to -12.09% in premarket trading ($152.25 as of 8:57 a.m. ET), after fiscal Q4 handset revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion and chip-design margins were guided down to 20-22% from 24% on rising memory and input costs, despite revenue of $10.4 billion beating the $10.1 billion expected. At least eight brokerages cut their price targets, per LSEG data.
headlines.why_it_matters: The memory-cost margin squeeze is now repricing the whole semi complex — Qualcomm's guide cut plus a wave of target cuts is what keeps the Nasdaq future down while the Dow rises.

headlines.headline: The chip selloff broadened in premarket trading: AMD -3.7%, Arm -3.6%, Marvell -3.3%, Micron -3%, Intel -2.7%, Broadcom -1.9%, TSMC -1.8%, while Nvidia steadied slightly to -1.42% ($197.29 as of 8:56 a.m. ET) from -1.80% at the 5 a.m. read. Data-center operators IREN, Hut 8 and Applied Digital fell 1.1-2.7%.
headlines.why_it_matters: The selling is concentrated in memory, handset and AI-infrastructure names rather than Nvidia itself — the tape is repricing the buildout's cost side, not the AI leader.

headlines.headline: AppLovin soared about 24% in premarket trading to $336.40 after Q3 revenue jumped 55% year over year to $2.18 billion (vs $2.07 billion expected) and EPS of $4.30 beat the $4.03 consensus; it guided Q4 revenue to $2.365-2.395 billion (vs $2.25 billion expected) and added $3.2 billion to its buyback authorization.
headlines.why_it_matters: A genuine ad-tech blowout with a raised guide is the morning's clearest counterweight to the chip selloff — it shows earnings can still lift a name sharply even on a down tape.

headlines.headline: Dutch Bros fell 14.53% in premarket trading to $37.60 even after beating Q3 estimates (EPS $0.25 vs $0.24 expected, revenue $549.84 million vs $547.41 million, same-shop sales +5.4%) because it cut its full-year 2026 revenue outlook. Cava fell about 8% premarket after missing revenue and earnings estimates, hurt by a Cyclospora outbreak and higher operating costs.
headlines.why_it_matters: A beat punished on a cut outlook — guidance, not the quarter, is what the market is trading this morning, in both directions.

headlines.headline: AI and data-center stocks slipped in premarket trading as the Democrats' sweeping midterm victory raised concerns about potential hurdles to the industry's rapid expansion, with growing public opposition in some key data-center states. Amazon, Alphabet and Meta were up nearly 1% each and Microsoft was flat, while Tesla fell about 1.9% premarket, extending its political slide.
headlines.why_it_matters: A new political overhang on the data-center buildout — distinct from the memory-cost story — is weighing on the infrastructure names while the hyperscalers that already own capacity keep their bid.

usac.why_it_matters: No fresh USAC news overnight; the Nov 3 Q3 story carries forward: record revenue $357.2M (+43% year over year, vs ~$348.32M consensus), record Adjusted EBITDA $197.3M, DCF coverage 1.67x, EPS $0.33 vs $0.3345 expected, distribution held at $0.525, full-year guidance tightened to Adjusted EBITDA $770-780M and DCF $495-505M. The $0.525 distribution pays tomorrow, Friday Nov 6. On the earnings call, management said over 60% of 2027 horsepower deliveries are contracted (about 90% of first-half deliveries), but flagged cost pressure: monthly lubricant costs exited Q3 about 25% above first-half levels and diesel hit an all-time high in September, with pricing not yet fully reflecting the increases.
